lessons.code:
# Class · Python with real data
import pandas as pd

sales = pd.read_csv("sales.csv")
mean = sales["amount"].mean()
print(f"Mean: {mean:.2f} €")
# → Mean: 48.73 €

# Class · Big Data with PySpark
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F

spark = SparkSession.builder.getOrCreate()
df = spark.read.parquet("data/sales/")
df.groupBy("country").agg(F.sum("amount")).show()
# → millions of rows, processed in parallel

# Class · Free AI with open models
# First, in the terminal: ollama pull llama3.2
import ollama

answer = ollama.chat(model="llama3.2", messages=[
    {"role": "user", "content": "What is a DataFrame?"},
])
print(answer["message"]["content"])
# → your own model, local and free

-- Class · Analytical SQL
SELECT country, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM sales
GROUP BY country
ORDER BY total DESC
LIMIT 5;
-- → the 5 best-selling markets

about.title: Learning is still a human thing
about.p1: IsAcademy was born from a simple idea: in an increasingly artificial world, real learning needs a person who listens, explains and challenges you.
about.p2: Founded by Ismael Sarmiento, a professional passionate about data and teaching, with over 10 years in the tech industry and over 10 years training professionals and teaching classes. We bring what companies actually do into every class, with patience, a personal approach and a plan tailored to each student.
about.p3: We use AI as a tool, never as a shortcut: we want you to understand what you do and to solve problems on your own.

method.title: Theory you understand, practice you apply
method.lead: We combine clear explanations, practice with real cases and challenges with visible progress (gamification), a very effective method to stay motivated and turn study into a habit.

pillars.d: Solid foundations explained clearly, no magic formulas. You'll know the why behind everything.
From the first class you work on real industry cases and projects, not filler exercises.
Clear goals and achievements that keep you motivated and turn study into a habit.

steps.d: In a first session we look at your starting point and what you want to achieve.
We design a roadmap for you: topics, pace and clear goals.
Every concept is worked through exercises and challenges, with just enough theory to understand it.
You apply what you learn in your own project, ready to show in class, in your thesis or in an interview.

facts: Python is named after the comedy group Monty Python, not the snake.
The most famous computer «bug» was a real moth stuck in a relay of the Harvard Mark II computer, in 1947.
SQL was born at IBM in the 1970s under the name SEQUEL.
The term «Artificial Intelligence» was coined in 1956, at the Dartmouth conference.
In the 19th century Ada Lovelace wrote what is considered the first algorithm intended for a machine.
Apache Spark started in 2009 as a research project at the University of California, Berkeley.
Hadoop is named after the toy elephant of one of its creators' son.
In 1997, IBM's Deep Blue beat world chess champion Garry Kasparov.
In 2016, AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol, one of the best Go players in the world.
Type «import this» in Python and you get the Zen of Python: 19 principles for writing good code.
The word «algorithm» comes from the name of the 9th-century Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi.
In 1950 Alan Turing proposed a test to tell whether a machine can imitate a human: the Turing test.
A byte has 8 bits, enough to represent 256 different values.
The relational model behind SQL databases was proposed by Edgar F. Codd in 1970.
The pandas library takes its name from «panel data», a data type used in econometrics.
Grace Hopper built one of the first compilers and championed programming with words instead of numbers.
Python was created by Guido van Rossum and first released in 1991.
Arthur Samuel popularised the term «machine learning» in 1959 with a program that learned to play checkers.
The perceptron, one of the first artificial neural networks, dates from 1958.
Much of a data scientist's work is cleaning and preparing data, not training models.
